summary: The note surveys the main policy debates ahead of the municipal elections on November 9, 2023. It covers housing, environment, public safety, economic development, education, and government transparency, matching candidates to their positions. It concludes that no single issue defines the race and that the outcome could set new precedent for local governance.
one_line: Overview of candidates' positions on housing, climate, policing, jobs, education, and transparency in the November 9, 2023 municipal elections.
key_facts: Municipal elections are scheduled for November 9, 2023.
Maria Gomez advocates loosening zoning laws for higher-density projects and streamlining approvals for new developments to lower housing costs.

Incumbent Mayor Richard Davies faces a tough re-election battle due to perceived inaction on housing; he proposes affordable housing mandates and incentives for developers who include low-income units.

Challenger Ellen Chu centers her campaign on environmental sustainability, proposing expanded public transportation, strict energy-efficiency building codes, and renewable energy for municipal buildings.
Thomas Erickson, a city council member running for mayor, is cautious about costs and promotes smaller-scale, community-driven green initiatives.
James Parker, a former police chief running for city council, wants a larger police budget to hire more officers and fund advanced crime prevention technologies.

Jasmine Lee, a social activist and city council candidate, wants to reallocate some police funding to mental health care, homelessness prevention, and youth programs, and focus on de-escalation and community policing.
Carlos Ramirez, a business owner running for mayor, proposes tax incentives and simpler regulation to attract businesses and create jobs.
Labor leader Sarah Johnson says Ramirez favors large corporations; she backs raising the minimum wage, strengthening workers' rights, and supporting small local businesses.
Kevin Zhao, a board of education trustee candidate, pushes investment in school technology and infrastructure and a curriculum overhaul.
Retired teacher Linda Schmidt, Zhao's opponent, emphasizes community support programs and after-school activities, and advocates more funding for them.
Sophie Rodriguez, a relative newcomer, promises open government, including a public portal to track municipal spending in real time and regular town hall meetings.
